explain.say: Next dot, the 1670s. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Dutch cloth seller, made tiny, powerful lenses. In pond water and in scrapings from his teeth he saw wriggling living things: the first bacteria anyone ever saw. Would you have believed him?

faq.a: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at cork through his microscope and saw tiny box-like spaces. He called them cells and drew them in his book Micrographia. They were the empty walls of dead plant cells.

Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, in the Netherlands, in the 1670s. His home-made single-lens microscopes magnified about 200 times or more, enough to see bacteria and single-celled creatures he called animalcules.
Cell theory says that all living things are made of one or more cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and, as Rudolf Virchow added in 1855, that new cells come only from existing cells.

faq.q: Why was the electron microscope invented?
faq.a: Light microscopes cannot show details smaller than about 0.2 micrometres. Electrons have a much shorter wavelength, so electron microscopes can show far smaller things, such as viruses and the insides of mitochondria.
asks: Tell me about the electron microscope

faq.q: Can an electron microscope look at living cells?
faq.a: Usually not. The sample sits in a vacuum and is often coated or frozen, so the cells are dead. Light microscopes are still used to watch living cells move and divide.
asks: Why do we still use light microscopes?

facts: Robert Hooke published drawings of cork cells in his book Micrographia in 1665.
Ernst Ruska and Max Knoll built the first electron microscope in Germany in 1931.

quiz.say: What did Hooke actually see in his slice of cork?
quiz.show: What did Hooke actually see in his slice of cork?

options.show: The walls of dead plant cells
options.say: The walls of dead plant cells

quiz.why: Cork is dead tissue, so Hooke saw only the empty cell walls, like a honeycomb.

wrong.0: Bacteria were first seen a few years later by Leeuwenhoek.
wrong.2: His microscope was not strong enough to show nuclei, and DNA was unknown then.

quiz.say: Why can an electron microscope see a virus when a light microscope cannot?
quiz.show: Why can an electron microscope see a virus when a light microscope cannot?

options.show: It uses electrons, which show much smaller detail
options.say: It uses electrons, which show much smaller detail

quiz.why: Electrons have a far shorter wavelength than light, so the image can show much finer detail.

wrong.0: Brighter light does not help; light itself cannot resolve such tiny things.
wrong.2: Colours in electron images are added later by computer; they do not make things visible.
